problem.title: Design a Real-Time Collaborative Document Editor (CRDTs & WebSockets)
problem.prompt: Design a Google Docs / Notion-style collaborative editor supporting 10M DAU, 100 concurrent editors per document, <80ms keystroke propagation, and seamless offline editing with automatic conflict-free merge on reconnect.

spark.summary: Building an offline-capable collaborative editor requires replacing central Operational Transformation (OT) locks with sequence CRDTs (RGA / Yjs) over sticky-routed WebSocket gateways, backed by an append-only operation log and periodic snapshot compaction.
spark.keyTakeaway: Sequence CRDTs guarantee strong eventual consistency without a central serialization server, but require tombstone compaction and delta-state encoding so document memory does not grow unboundedly.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Concurrent offline edits break naive index-based updates (`insert(pos=5, 'x')`). **Sequence CRDTs** (such as RGA or Yjs) assign each character a globally unique, causally ordered ID `(lamport_ts, client_id)` so concurrent inserts merge **commutatively** in any delivery order.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts `Client A (Offline Edit)` and `Client B (Concurrent Edit)` each maintaining a local `RGA / Yjs Character Tree` (`a1@A`, `b1@B`), exchanging deltas through a `WebSocket Pub/Sub Gateway` with `Commutative Merge (Zero Locks)` and persisting to a `Compacted Snapshot Store + Op Log`.

**Trade-Offs & Production:** CRDTs eliminate central OT transform-server bottlenecks and support peer-to-peer/offline merges, at the cost of tombstone metadata overhead—mitigated via run-length block encoding and background GC compaction.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Hash-route document rooms to stateful WebSocket/Redis-PubSub shards, enforce per-document max op-size limits, and compact op logs every N=1,000 edits.

learningJourney.title: Clarify Concurrency, Offline Sync & Latency Math
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: size WebSocket connections, delta broadcast fanout, and op-log storage.
learningJourney.explanation: With **10M DAU** and ~500K concurrent active sockets, each typing editor emits ~3–5 keystrokes/sec (~100 bytes per binary CRDT delta). Broadcasting to 100 peers in a room requires `<80 ms` p99 fanout, while offline editors must buffer thousands of local edits and merge cleanly upon reconnect without losing cursor intent.

learningJourney.title: Why Operational Transformation (OT) Needs a Central Arbiter
learningJourney.purpose: The failure mode: compare central OT index-shifting against lock-free CRDT convergence.
learningJourney.explanation: Classic **OT** transforms integer offsets (`insert(5, 'a')`) on a single authoritative server per document. Supporting multi-hour **offline editing** or multi-region active-active rooms in OT becomes notoriously bug-prone (`TP2` puzzle). **Sequence CRDTs (RGA / Yjs)** anchor every insert to its *left/right neighbor's immutable ID*, making merges associative, commutative, and idempotent.

learningJourney.title: RGA/Yjs Delta Sync + Sticky WebSocket Shards + Op-Log Compaction
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: route document rooms via consistent hashing and compact tombstones asynchronously.
learningJourney.explanation: Consistent-hash `doc_id` to a **WebSocket Room Shard** (with Redis Pub/Sub cross-pod fanout for failover). Clients exchange **state vectors** (`{clientId: maxClock}`) on reconnect to fetch only missing binary deltas, while a background compactor merges the append-only op log into a single **base snapshot** and garbage-collects deleted tombstones once all active replicas acknowledge the epoch.

cards.label: State-Vector Sync
cards.detail: Reconnects exchange compact version vectors to stream only missing deltas.

cards.label: Run-Length Blocks
cards.detail: Yjs merges contiguous typing by one author into 1 block, cutting RAM 10x.

cards.label: Safe Compaction
cards.detail: Squashes op logs into a base snapshot periodically for fast cold loads.

sectionDiagram.summary: Caption: Sticky document rooms broadcast tiny binary CRDT deltas in <80ms while background compaction bounds op-log and tombstone growth.

learningJourney.title: Taming Tombstone Bloat & Ephemeral Cursor Presence
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: keep deleted characters and live cursors from bloating persistent state.
learningJourney.explanation: Never persist live cursor/selection coordinates in the CRDT op log—broadcast **awareness/presence** as ephemeral volatile messages over WebSockets with a 30s TTL. For deleted text, compress consecutive deletions into run-length **tombstone ranges** and run periodic snapshot compaction.

learningJourney.title: Permissions Revocation, Undo/Redo & Large Document Splitting
learningJourney.purpose: Applied problems: enforce access control on reconnect and keep per-user undo local.
learningJourney.explanation: On permission downgrade, immediately close the WebSocket and reject delta writes at the room gateway; implement **local per-user undo** using inverse operations scoped strictly to `client_id` so `Ctrl+Z` never undoes a collaborator's edits.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why do sequence CRDTs (RGA / Yjs) anchor character insertions to neighbor IDs like (lamport_ts, client_id) instead of integer array indexes?

options.text: Immutable neighbor IDs make concurrent inserts commutative and idempotent regardless of delivery order or offline duration
options.feedback: Correct: integer indexes shift under concurrent edits, whereas unique causal IDs always resolve to the same total order across all replicas.

options.text: Because JavaScript arrays cannot store more than 1,000 characters
options.feedback: Incorrect: the issue is concurrent index invalidation, not array size.

options.text: To force every keystroke through a two-phase commit
options.feedback: Incorrect: CRDTs avoid synchronous 2PC locks completely.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if a CRDT-backed editor never compacts deleted characters (tombstones)?

options.text: Document metadata and cold-load latency grow monotonically with total historical edits, even if the visible text stays short
options.feedback: Correct: tombstones remain in the causal tree until compacted into a fresh base snapshot.

options.text: Deleted characters reappear randomly for other users
options.feedback: Incorrect: tombstones preserve correctness, they just consume memory and load time.

options.text: WebSockets automatically switch to HTTP/1.0 polling
options.feedback: Incorrect: tombstone bloat affects memory/storage, not transport negotiation.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should live collaborator cursor positions be stored?

options.text: In an ephemeral in-memory presence/awareness channel (not persisted in the durable CRDT op log)
options.feedback: Correct: cursor moves happen dozens of times per second and have zero durability value after disconnect.

options.text: In the durable SQLite/Postgres op log so every cursor move can be replayed
options.feedback: Incorrect: persisting ephemeral cursor moves would explode op-log storage and compaction overhead.
Incorrect: DNS is not a real-time presence channel.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
